items.prompt: Average-case lookup by key in a well-spread hash map is?
items.whyRight: A good hash plus load factor keeps buckets short, so expected work is constant.
whyWrong: Logarithmic cost is trees or sorted structures, not the average hash story.
Linear is the collapse when everything collides into one bucket.
n log n is sorting territory.

items.prompt: Worst-case lookup when every key hashes to the same bucket (naive chaining) is?
items.whyRight: You walk a chain of length n.
whyWrong: Constant time assumes the hash spreads; it does not hold under total collision.
Treeified buckets can restore log n, but the classic chaining answer is linear.
Square root is not the collision bound.

items.prompt: You need existence checks for n integers with expected O(1). First structure to name?
whyWrong: Sorted array membership is log n via binary search.
A list membership scan is linear.
Unbalanced trees can degrade to linear.

items.prompt: Why can a mutable object used as a map key be dangerous?
choices: Changing fields that affect equals/hashCode loses the entry in the wrong bucket
Hashing requires keys to be integers
items.whyRight: The map placed the entry under the old hash; mutating the key breaks findability.
whyWrong: Object keys are normal when hash/equals are stable.
Load factor is about size vs capacity, not key mutation.

items.prompt: Two-sum in O(n) typically stores what in the hash map?
choices: Value → index of numbers seen so far
A sorted copy of the array
items.whyRight: As you scan, look up target − x; store x after the check.
whyWrong: Materializing every pair is quadratic space/time.
Sorting first changes the algorithm (two pointers) and is not the hash path.

items.prompt: Load factor grows past the threshold. What does a typical map do?
choices: Allocate a larger table and rehash entries
Switch permanently to linear search of a list
whyWrong: Random deletes are not the resize policy.
Falling back to one giant list would destroy the average bound.
Rejecting inserts is not standard map behavior.
